title: Transport Signatures of a Kinetically Self-Trapped Nagaoka Polaron
abstract: Nagaoka polarons are canonical examples of kinetic magnetism. Although their spin structure is well understood, their transport remains unexplored. We compute the dynamical mobility of a single hole in the square-lattice $t$-model using resummation-based quantum Monte Carlo and analytic continuation. Upon cooling, an incoherent Drude-like response gives way to a finite-frequency peak as the dc mobility vanishes. The peak signals an internal mode of a hole confined by its ferromagnetic cloud. Our results establish transport as an incisive probe of polaron formation and kinetic self-trapping.
summary: This work calculates the transport properties of the Nagaoka polaron in the t-model using advanced Quantum Monte Carlo techniques. The key finding is that as the system cools, the transport signature shifts from metallic to insulating, marked by a distinct finite-frequency peak. This demonstrates that transport measurements are a sensitive probe of kinetic self-trapping in correlated electron systems.
main_problem: The paper investigates the previously unexplored transport properties of the Nagaoka polaron, a key concept in kinetic magnetism.
main_result: The dynamical mobility transitions from a Drude-like response to an insulating state characterized by a finite-frequency peak, signaling the internal mode of the hole confined by its ferromagnetic cloud.
method: The study employs resummation-based Quantum Monte Carlo simulations combined with stochastic analytic continuation to calculate the dynamical mobility.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a single hole moving in the square-lattice t-model, which exhibits polaron formation and kinetic self-trapping.
key_observables: Dynamical mobility $\mu(\omega)$, DC mobility $\mu_{	ext{DC}}$, and the finite-frequency peak in $\mu(\omega)$.
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), magnetic field (Zeeman field), and the lattice hopping parameter ($t$).
main_assumptions: The calculation relies on mapping the problem to a Bethe lattice model and using resummation techniques to efficiently compute current correlation functions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the thermal evolution of $\mu(\omega)$ showing the transition to the peak, and the effect of an external magnetic field on melting this polaron state.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework using QMC on a Bethe lattice, then calculates the dynamical mobility, and finally analyzes the temperature and field dependence to characterize polaron formation and melting.
why_interesting: The connection between transport measurements (dynamical mobility) and the underlying electronic structure (polaron formation) provides a powerful diagnostic tool for understanding strongly correlated phases, which is relevant to understanding exotic quantum materials.
